claims.text: Machine-learning interatomic potentials can be used with two-phase coexistence molecular dynamics to predict the melting properties of high-melting refractory materials.
The predicted properties include melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
The proposed method significantly reduces computational cost relative to ab initio free-energy calculations.
NbMoTaW is an example of a high-melting refractory high-entropy alloy applicable to the proposed method.
The initial refractory material is solid under ambient conditions.
ML-potential-driven molecular dynamics can replace ab initio molecular-dynamics thermodynamic integration for direct two-phase coexistence simulations.
Constant-pressure simulations over temperatures spanning the expected melting point can be used to study phase coexistence.
Equilibrating an initially prepared solid-liquid interface can establish solid-liquid coexistence.
A stable solid-liquid interface serves as the structural mediator for determining melting properties.
An ML potential trained on DFT data can replicate the ab initio energy landscape.
The ML potential evaluates the energy landscape at substantially lower computational expense than ab initio calculations.
Solid-liquid interfacial dynamics in a two-phase coexistence simulation permit determination of the melting temperature.
Energy changes between the solid and liquid phases can be used to determine enthalpy of fusion.
Entropy of fusion can be derived from the enthalpy of fusion and melting temperature.
Simulation-cell volume differences between the solid and liquid phases can be used to determine the volume change at melting.
ML-potential two-phase molecular dynamics is expected to predict melting properties within approximately 5–10% of ab initio free-energy results.
The anticipated computational savings would be sufficient to support high-throughput studies.
Accuracy near melting depends critically on representing high-energy configurations in the ML training dataset.
An ML potential may deviate from DFT predictions under extreme conditions if its training dataset is not representative of melting behavior.
Systematic benchmarking across multiple material systems is required to establish the quantitative error and computational advantage of the method.
